sections.h2: Does Kentucky tax house sale profit separately?
sections.html:
No. Kentucky has no capital gains schedule. KRS 141.020 levies one flat percentage on the entire net income of a resident, so profit from a Kentucky closing simply joins the rest of that year's income.

With a flat state rate, the big variable for a Kentucky seller is how much profit is left after the federal rules apply. A longtime homeowner may shield nearly all of it. A landlord, a flipper or an heir who sells an inherited house usually cannot. Ask the Kentucky Department of Revenue how an excluded gain is carried onto Form 740 before you file.

sections.h2: Kentucky income tax rate by year
sections.html:
A closing in a taxable year beginning on or after January 1, 2026 is taxed at 3.5 percent of net income. The rate has stepped down several times, so the year of the closing matters.

Kentucky individual income tax rate by taxable year (KRS 141.020)
Taxable years beginningRate on net income
2018 through 20225 percent
20234.5 percent
2024 and 20254 percent
2026 and after3.5 percent

Further cuts for 2027 and later years depend on budget triggers and a vote of the General Assembly. The statute bars the department from lowering the rate by itself, so do not count on a lower rate when you pick a closing date.

Federal law lets a seller shield up to $250,000 of profit on a main home, or $500,000 on a joint return. Two tests apply, and both are measured over the five years that end on the closing date.

  • Ownership: you or your spouse held title for two years or more.
  • Use: you lived there as a residence for two years or more. On a joint return, each spouse must meet this test personally.
  • The two-year spans can fall at different points inside the five-year window.
  • A seller who shielded profit on a different home during the two years before this closing generally cannot claim it again.
  • Members of the Uniformed Services, the Foreign Service and the intelligence community on qualified extended duty may freeze the five-year window for as long as a decade.

A Form 1099-S from the closing agent creates a duty to report the sale even if no tax is due. Reporting is also required whenever part of the profit is left over after the shield.

Profit is the net amount you realize at closing minus your adjusted basis. Basis begins with the purchase price plus sales tax and buying costs. It rises with improvements that add value and falls with depreciation claimed and insurance money received for casualty or theft losses.

If you put a new roof or a finished basement into a Kentucky house, keep those invoices. Each one lifts basis and trims the taxable profit. An heir or a recipient of a gift follows different basis rules, explained in IRS Publication 551. A house held for one year or less produces short-term gain, taxed like wages, while a longer hold produces long-term gain.

A loss on a home you lived in cannot be deducted. A sale below basis gives no write-off.

sections.h2: Federal tax on profit above the shield
sections.html:
Long-term profit lands in one of three federal tiers, zero, fifteen or twenty percent, set by taxable income and filing status. The cutoffs are republished each year in IRS Topic no. 409, so read the table for your closing year instead of trusting an old figure.

Depreciation changes the picture for rentals. The slice of profit that reflects depreciation on real property (unrecaptured section 1250 gain) can be taxed at up to 25 percent federally. Reporting runs through Form 8949 and Schedule D.

A house you never lived in fails the use test, so the main-home shield is generally unavailable. Depreciation you took reduces basis and raises profit, and a rental that has run for years can produce a large number even when the market barely moved.

An inherited house raises two separate questions. One is income tax on profit above basis, which follows Publication 551. The other is Kentucky inheritance tax, a levy on the heir's right to receive property under KRS Chapter 140 that has nothing to do with your Form 740. Class A heirs, such as a spouse, child or sibling, are exempt from that second tax.

  • Pull depreciation schedules before listing, not after closing.
  • Ask the estate's personal representative for the valuation papers used on the estate return.
  • Choose a closing date with the tax year and its rate in mind.

Because the rate depends on the taxable year, a closing in late December and one in early January can land in different years. Look at your other income for each year, any credits you rely on and the date the two-year use test is met. If you are a few weeks short of two years in the home, waiting can turn a taxable gain into a shielded one. Talk to a tax preparer before signing a contract with a firm closing date.

sections.h2: Sellers who live outside Kentucky or moved during the year
sections.html:
A nonresident owes Kentucky tax on income from tangible property in Kentucky, and a house here counts as that property. KRS 141.020 also taxes a part-year resident as a resident for the months of residency and as a nonresident for the remaining months.

The Department of Revenue prints Form 740 and Form 740-NP. Ask the department which return fits your move date, because that choice decides whether the whole profit or only the Kentucky-sourced part is reported.

sections.h2: Credits a large sale can affect
sections.html:
Kentucky offers a $40 credit for each person aged 65 or over and for a legally blind individual, and a $20 credit for Kentucky National Guard members. A nonrefundable family size tax credit under KRS 141.066 is tied to modified gross income and family size, with a 2025 ceiling of $42,760.

A closing can lift modified gross income for the year, so a household that normally qualifies for the family size credit may lose it in a sale year. Run the numbers with the closing profit included before you decide on the sale date.

Collect the records that fix basis and residency now, because the closing agent's Form 1099-S shows only the sale price. A short list saves a preparer hours later.

  • The closing statement from your own purchase, showing cost and buying expenses.
  • Receipts for work that added value, such as a roof, an addition or a finished basement.
  • Depreciation schedules if any part of the house produced rent.
  • Proof of the dates you lived there, such as utility bills and the address on your license.
  • For an inherited house, the estate valuation papers and the personal representative's letters.

A taxable profit may call for estimated tax payments during the year. Ask the Department of Revenue whether Kentucky estimated payments apply to your sale year, and set aside part of the proceeds.

faqs.q: Does Kentucky give a break for selling a main home?
faqs.a: Kentucky has no home sale break of its own. The federal shield of $250,000 single or $500,000 joint controls how much profit you have, so confirm with the Department of Revenue how it appears on Form 740.

faqs.q: What rate will Kentucky charge on my profit for a 2026 closing?
faqs.a: The rate is 3.5 percent of net income for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, the same percentage that applies to wages.

faqs.q: Do I report the sale if the whole profit is shielded?
faqs.a: Yes, when you receive a Form 1099-S or when any portion of the profit is left over. Use Form 8949 and Schedule D where they apply.

faqs.q: Can I write off a loss on a house I lived in?
faqs.a: No. Losses on personal-use property such as a home are not deductible.

faqs.q: Does someone who lives in another state owe Kentucky tax on selling a Kentucky house?
faqs.a: Yes. Kentucky taxes a nonresident's income from tangible property in the state. Ask the department which return applies and how credits are prorated.
